title: EMDR: How Eye Movement Therapy Treats Trauma
description: EMDR therapy uses eye movements to process traumatic memories. How it works, what sessions look like, effectiveness research, and who it helps.

content.text: EMDR sounds strange—following a therapist's finger with your eyes to heal trauma. But it's one of the most evidence-based treatments for PTSD. Here's how it works.
EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) helps the brain process traumatic memories so they no longer trigger intense distress.
Trauma gets 'stuck' in the brain's memory network, stored with all the original emotions and sensations. EMDR appears to help the brain reprocess these memories into normal narrative memories.
While focusing on the traumatic memory, you follow alternating stimulation:

items: The specific method matters less than the alternation

content.text: Building rapport, identifying target memories, teaching coping skills for distress.

items: Identify negative belief about self ('I'm not safe')
Focus on memory while doing bilateral stimulation
Notice what comes up (images, thoughts, sensations)

content.text: Returning to calm, homework for between sessions, reviewing progress.
Meta-analyses show EMDR is as effective as trauma-focused CBT (Prolonged Exposure, CPT) for PTSD, with some evidence it works faster.
EMDR is recommended as a first-line treatment for PTSD by the WHO, VA/DoD, and APA.

items: Similar effectiveness to Prolonged Exposure and CPT
May involve less homework than PE/CPT
Less explicit verbal processing of trauma
Some do EMDR online (evidence supports this)

content.text: EMDR is a well-researched trauma treatment that works differently from talk therapy. If you've experienced trauma and want an alternative to prolonged exposure, EMDR is worth exploring. It's not magic, but for many people, it provides relief that years of traditional therapy couldn't.
